opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I don't think there's a fully satisfying explanation, but I can give a few intuitions.

One way to think about it is that a bigger model contains a larger ensemble of circuits or "programs" that could implement the function you're trying to learn. With more parameters, there's a better chance that some sub-network is already close to the right computation, and gradient descent just has to find it and amplify it, rather than build it from scratch. That's sort of the lottery-ticket-style intuition: more tickets, more likely one of them is already a winner, so you need fewer examples to pick it out.

Another angle is that larger models learn better, more general representations during pre-training. If you've already got a rich set of features (concepts, abstractions, ways of decomposing problems), then learning a new task is mostly about composing things you already have. You need much less data to learn a mapping on top of good features than to learn the features themselves. So a lot of the sample efficiency you see in fine-tuning or in-context learning is really inherited from the pre-training compute.

There's also an optimization story. In a bigger network, the loss landscape is in some sense smoother or better conditioned; there are more directions you can move to reduce loss without messing up other things. So each gradient step on an example can make more progress, and there's less interference between what you're learning now and what you learned before.

I'd add that "sample-efficient" is a bit slippery, because part of what's happening is that larger models can simply memorize and integrate a single example more effectively. They have the capacity to store a fact after seeing it once or twice, whereas a small model has to compress and might just not retain it.

But honestly, I'd put all of these in the category of plausible stories rather than a rigorous theory. We have the empirical scaling laws that clearly show it, and we have these intuitions, but I don't think anyone has a really crisp first-principles derivation of why it works out the way it does.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's one of those things where I think we have a decent intuitive story, but I'm not sure anyone has a fully satisfying answer.

The way I think about it is that a bigger model has a lot more circuits, or sub-computations, that it can bring to bear on any given problem. So when it sees a new piece of data, it has more hypotheses it's already representing internally, and it's more likely that one of them is close to the right thing. Then the gradient update just has to slightly upweight that circuit rather than build it from scratch. A small model, by contrast, has to actually carve out the computation through many steps of gradient descent, because nothing it already has is a good match. So you end up with a picture where the big model is doing something closer to search over a rich library of existing features, and the small model is doing something closer to constructing features slowly.

Another way to say it is that large models are better at reusing what they've learned. If you've seen a lot of math and a lot of code, and then you see a new kind of reasoning problem, a big model can compose things it already knows and get most of the way there with very little additional data. A small model has to be more specialized, so every new task looks more like a fresh learning problem.

There's also the more formal angle, where if you think about these models as approximating something like Bayesian inference, a larger model is closer to the ideal learner that puts mass on all the plausible hypotheses and updates efficiently. Smaller models are a worse approximation to that, so they need more samples to get the same amount of information out of the data.

And then I'd add that, with fine-tuning and RL in particular, you see this really clearly. A bigger pretrained model often needs far fewer examples to pick up a new behavior, because the behavior is almost already there — you're just eliciting it, or steering it, rather than teaching it. That's part of why so much of the practical work has shifted toward getting the base model good and then using relatively small amounts of high quality data on top. The sample efficiency of the big model is what makes that whole recipe work.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we have a fully satisfying explanation. But one intuition is that a larger model can learn more from each example because it can pick up on more of the structure in it. A single piece of text contains information about syntax, facts, reasoning, and lots of other things. A smaller model might only be able to capture a few of those patterns, whereas a larger model can capture more of them simultaneously.

There’s also a distinction between sample efficiency during pretraining and sample efficiency when you’re teaching the model a new task. In the second case, the larger model may already have most of the relevant capabilities. You just need a few examples to indicate which capability you want it to use. So what looks like learning something from very little data is partly drawing on things it learned earlier.

But that still leaves the underlying question of why scale helps you learn those representations in the first place. I think those intuitions are useful, but I wouldn’t claim they’re a complete explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we have a fully satisfying explanation. One intuition is that a larger model can pick up more of the structure in the data, so each example teaches it more. An example isn’t just evidence about one particular fact—it contains information about language, about concepts, and about how those concepts relate. A model with more capacity can make use of more of those signals.

There’s also a distinction between sample efficiency and compute efficiency. If you hold the number of training examples fixed, a bigger model generally does better, but it’s spending more computation on each example. So part of the answer might simply be that you’re doing more computation to extract information from the same data. The interesting question is why that extra computation is so reliably useful, and I don’t think we understand that completely.
